ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is the ability of microbes to survive drugs that normally kill them, driven by genetic changes and spread via plasmids. Clinicians must recognise patterns, use diagnostics wisely, and choose agents that overcome resistance while preserving future options.

sections.p: AMR occurs when bacteria acquire mechanisms—enzymatic inactivation, target alteration, efflux pumps, or reduced permeability—that render standard antibiotics ineffective. Diagnosis relies on culture and susceptibility testing, comparing isolate MICs to breakpoints.
b: Identify resistant organism by culture + susceptibility
Use local antibiogram to interpret results

t.b: Result shows susceptible, intermediate, or resistant; guides drug choice

sections.p: Severity is gauged by infection site, host factors, and resistance level. The CDC’s 3‑tier classification (susceptible, multidrug‑resistant, pan‑resistant) helps triage urgency and infection control measures.
b: Multidrug‑resistant: non‑susceptibility to ≥1 agent in ≥3 classes

sections.p: Resistance emerges from selective pressure of inappropriate or excessive antibiotic use, then spreads via plasmid conjugation. In low‑resource settings, common drivers include unregulated over‑the‑counter antibiotics, sub‑therapeutic dosing, and co‑infection with TB, HIV, malaria, or hepatitis B that prompts frequent courses.

Patients present with standard infection signs (fever, pain, purulence) but fail to improve despite appropriate‑dose therapy, suggesting a resistant pathogen. Look for recurrent infections, recent antibiotic exposure, or travel to high‑resistance regions.
b: Persistent fever after 48‑72 h of therapy

sections.p: Targeted testing confirms resistance and guides therapy. When labs are unavailable, use clinical algorithms and local resistance data.

t.a: Rapid molecular PCR for resistance genes
t.b: Positive → likely resistant to that class; negative does not rule out other mechanisms
Guides empiric choice while awaiting susceptibility

sections.p: Untreated resistant infections can progress to sepsis, organ failure, or death, especially in immunocompromised hosts or neonates. Early escalation is critical.

Treat the identified pathogen with an agent that overcomes the resistance mechanism, then provide supportive care. Choose drugs based on PK/PD principles—time‑dependent vs concentration‑dependent—and avoid agents with high toxicity or known drug‑drug interactions in the patient.
b: Beta‑lactamase inhibitor combos for ESBL producers
Vancomycin or linezolid for MRSA (target‑site alteration)
Use carbapenems sparingly to preserve efficacy

sections.p: Re‑culture after 48‑72 h to confirm clearance, adjust therapy based on response, and monitor for adverse effects. Prevent future AMR by antimicrobial stewardship, infection control, and patient education.
b: Stewardship: narrow spectrum once susceptibilities known
Hand hygiene, isolation for MDR organisms

sections.p: Treatment failure due to poor drug absorption, inadequate source control, or non‑infectious inflammation can mimic AMR.
MICs near breakpoints may be misinterpreted; some resistance mechanisms (e.g., efflux) are not detected by standard susceptibility panels, leading to false susceptibility reports.
b: Consider synergy testing for inducible resistance

whenToSeekHelp: Septic shock, organ dysfunction, or rapid clinical deterioration despite appropriate therapy

faq.q: Why does a bacterium become resistant to a drug it was once susceptible to?
faq.a: Selective pressure from antibiotic exposure favors survival of mutants or acquired genes that neutralise, expel, or evade the drug.

faq.q: Can resistance be reversed once it develops?
faq.a: Stopping selective pressure can reduce resistant strains, but genetic changes often persist; prudent use slows spread.

faq.q: How do I choose an empiric antibiotic in a setting with high AMR?
faq.a: Use local antibiogram data, consider infection source, patient risk factors, and select agents with activity against likely resistant organisms.

exam: Explain the four main mechanisms by which bacteria develop antimicrobial resistance and give a clinical example for each.
Interpret a susceptibility report that shows an ESBL‑producing E. coli and outline the appropriate antibiotic class and stewardship considerations.
Describe how you would manage a patient with suspected carbapenem‑resistant Enterobacteriaceae infection in a low‑resource hospital.
